IMPORTANT: Other agents are working in this same checkout at the same time. You MUST NOT change the state of the git branch: do NOT run `git checkout`, `git switch`, `git stash`, `git reset`, `git restore`, `git rebase`, `git merge`, `git pull`, `git cherry-pick`, or `git commit --amend`, and do NOT create, delete, or rename branches. Doing any of these will interfere with the other running agents. If you spawn sub-agents, include this rule in their instructions.

Do an adversarial code review of the current branch. This is a read-only review; do NOT push to GitHub or modify existing commits.
Base commit: aaa111
HEAD commit: bbb222

Setup:
- Use the GitHub MCP tools (`mcp__github__*`, load via ToolSearch if needed) to check for PR metadata: title, body, head SHA, base, CI status, and comments. The branch may not have been pushed or have an open PR yet; these are useful optional context, not required fields.
- Read any relevant `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` files for context.
- Read all of the code changes between the branch's base commit and the HEAD commit.

Spawn a pool of six Sonnet sub-agents to examine each of the following aspects of the code changes in parallel:

### Design
- Is this the best approach to accomplish what the code is trying to do?
- Is this code sustainable? Is it a design that can easily grow over time, or will it lock us into a potentially problematic pattern as we scale and the code evolves?
- Suggest better solutions if any exist.

### Abstraction
- Is this the right place for this change to live?
- Does this code own the data that it's modifying?
- If we're passing parameters, would it make more sense for them to be member data of the object that's being operated on instead?
- Does this change increase the number of files we'll have to touch the next time this functionality has to change?
- Is there a deeper structural change we could make that would make this change simpler?

### Code quality
- Unclear code, where the intent isn't obvious from the code itself and no comments explain it
- Useless comments that just explain what the code is doing without explaining why
- Misspellings in variable names or comments
- Ignoring established patterns that already exist in the codebase
- Places where necessary error handling is missing, or errors are being unnecessarily suppressed
- Stale comments, docstrings, or skills that no longer accurately describe the code

### Performance
- Inefficient procedures (O(n^2) algorithms, duplicated work, etc.)
- Database queries that are likely to be problematic
- Excessive queries to databases or APIs which could be batched into fewer queries
- Memory leaks, or large memory allocations that don't get freed by garbage collection
- Inefficient, money-wasting use of LLM tokens or cloud resources
- Anything else that could be unexpectedly slow or resource-intensive

### Security
- Do the changes potentially introduce any security holes that an attacker could use to leak data, impersonate users, escalate privileges, run untrusted commands, or cause any other unwanted security violation?
- You MUST include an explanation of why it worries you and a description of how an attacker could make use of it. Only report an issue if you can describe a concrete, realistic attack: what specific input or action the attacker takes, what system boundary they cross, and what they gain. Speculative chains of events ("could potentially lead to...") do not qualify.
- Code quality concerns, error handling gaps, and reliability issues are NOT security findings unless they directly enable a violation with no additional assumptions.
- For each candidate finding, argue against it: what would have to be true for this to actually be exploitable? If the preconditions are implausible or outside an attacker's control, discard it.

### Testing
Work mainly by reading code. You may run at most 3 test commands, and each must target only the test files that cover the changed source files; never run the full suite. Do NOT do mutation testing, copy the repository, or modify any files to see whether tests fail; reason about it from the code instead.

Prioritize, in this order, and stop when you run out of time:
1. Tests changed on this branch only to make them pass, while the bug that they found is still in the code. Examples: an expected value changed to match incorrect output, an assertion removed or made less strict, a test skipped or deleted, or an error that the test now ignores. For each changed assertion, decide from the code and the requirements if the new expected behaviour is correct. If it is not, report the bug that the old test found.
2. Changed logic that has branches or error paths with no test that exercises them.
3. Changed behaviour whose existing tests would still pass if the change were reverted.
4. Tests changed on this branch that are brittle (timing, ordering, over-mocking) or don't provide enough protection to be worthwhile.
5. Pre-existing tests that the change made irrelevant.
Skip anything outside the changed files and their direct callers.

Time budget: 10 minutes. Run `date` when you start and record the time, then check `date` periodically. When the budget is used up, stop investigating and report what you have.

Give each sub-agent the full text of its section above, including any limits, without paraphrasing it.

Instructions for each sub-agent: "Hunt adversarially. Try to break the code. VERIFY every candidate issue before including it. Cite file:line at the PR head, quote the code or prompt text, and drop anything you can't substantiate. Classify each finding with the severity rubric below, and include one sentence that explains why you chose that level. Each one gets a title, a file:line link (https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/bbb222/path#Lnn), evidence, a concrete failing example where relevant, and a suggested fix."

Give each sub-agent the full text of the severity rubric below, without paraphrasing it.

### Severity rubric
Rate each finding on its impact on users and on the codebase if this branch merges as it is now. Do not rate it on your confidence: if you cannot verify a finding, drop it; if you can verify it, rate it on its impact.
- Blocker: Merging causes a real defect on a realistic path: incorrect results, data loss or corruption, a crash or hang, a security hole, a regression in existing behaviour, or a broken build or test suite. A design that will be expensive to undo once other code depends on it is also a Blocker. Ask: "If this were my PR, would I refuse to merge it until this is fixed?" If yes, it is a Blocker.
- Should Fix: A real problem that does not cause a defect now, or causes one only on an unlikely path. Examples: missing error handling for a rare case, changed logic with no test, a misleading comment, a performance problem that does not matter at the current scale.
- Nit: No effect on behaviour or maintainability. Examples: naming, wording, formatting, small cleanups.

For testing findings:
- A test changed to hide a bug gets the severity of the bug that it hides.
- A changed branch or error path with no test is Should Fix.
- It is a Blocker if the untested path also contains a suspected bug, or if a bug there could cause data loss or a security hole.
- It is a Nit only if the path has no logic of its own (for example, it only logs a message).

Deliverable: write `.gv-review/code-review-findings.md` containing:
- Title, PR link (if any), head SHA, base SHA, today's date in `YYYY-MM-DD` format, and a one-line scope.
- A one-line verdict, plus counts of Blockers / Should Fix / Nits.
- Findings grouped by severity as Blockers, Should Fix, and Nits.
Keep it tight. Do not put any model names in the file. If the file already exists, replace it — the pre-existing contents are no longer useful.

Before you write each version of the file, rate every finding again against the severity rubric. The sub-agents' ratings are only suggestions. Merge duplicate findings. Then derive the verdict from the ratings:
- One or more Blockers: "Do not merge."
- No Blockers, but one or more Should Fix: "Merge after fixes."
- Only Nits, or no findings: "OK to merge."
If you think the branch must not merge but no finding is a Blocker, find the finding that causes your concern and make it a Blocker, or add it as a new finding.

Do not wait for all sub-agents before you write the file. Each time a sub-agent reports, rewrite the file with all findings received so far, and put `Partial: waiting on <aspects>` under the title, listing the aspects that have not reported yet. When all six have reported, remove that line.
